Example lessons for Grade 8 US History. Each one pairs a MapMaker map with an inquiry, a Word student sheet in English and Spanish, and teacher notes.

Drafts: not yet reviewed 10 lessons · US History

• October

    1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

    US History · Grade 8 · Road to revolution and the Revolution

    Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • November

    Presidential Elections, 1796 and 1800

    US History · Grade 8 · The early republic

    Compare how each state's electors voted in 1796 and 1800, see which states changed sides, and find two Supreme Court cases that shaped the new government.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • November

    Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live

    US History · Grade 8 · The Bill of Rights and citizenship

    Map the public places in your own community where people use the rights in the Bill of Rights and carry out their responsibilities as citizens, and find who represents your district in Congress.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • November

    The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

    US History · Grade 8 · The early republic

    Compare the Louisiana Purchase with the United States of 1803, see why the Mississippi River and New Orleans mattered, and follow Lewis and Clark's route across rivers and biomes to the Pacific.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • November

    The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

    US History · Grade 8 · The early republic

    Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • November

    We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791

    US History · Grade 8 · The Constitution

    See how House seats were shared out after the 1790 census, how the three-fifths clause changed the count, and how close each state's vote to ratify was.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • February

    Roads, Trails, and Rails West

    US History · Grade 8 · Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

    Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • March

    US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

    US History · Grade 8 · Reform and the road to war

    Compare free and slave states in 1850, follow the routes of the internal slave trade south, and trace the Underground Railroad north to freedom.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • April

    Civil War Battlefields

    US History · Grade 8 · The Civil War

    See how the United States split in 1861, compare the railroads of the North and the South, and find where the war's battles were fought.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

  • April

    The Battle of Vicksburg

    US History · Grade 8 · The Civil War

    Follow Grant's 1863 march to Vicksburg along the Mississippi River, and see why taking the city split the Confederacy in two.

    Draft: not yet reviewed

Lessons › US History

1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.

  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • UnitRoad to revolution and the Revolution
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Share to Google Classroom (opens in a new tab) Student activity Teacher notes

Draft: not yet reviewed Content version 0.3.0, updated 2026-10-13.

About this map

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Revolutionary War BattlesWhat it shows: 21 battles from April 1775 to December 1776. Each pop-up gives the dates, a picture and a short account of the battle. The symbol color shows the winner, as listed in the legend (American victory or British victory).Source: American Battlefield Trust
Revolutionary War BattlefieldsWhat it shows: Battlefield boundaries, and the core areas where the fighting was heaviestSource: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program
Turning PointsWhat it shows: Five events, from Lexington and Concord to Trenton, with short notesSource: Chris Bunin and Peter Trentacoste (2026), from National Park Service, US Army Center of Military History and Library of Congress sources
Thirteen British ColoniesWhat it shows: Colony borders in 1763Source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988)
1763 Proclamation LineWhat it shows: The line west of which King George III barred colonial settlementSource: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988)
Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Ports that supplied armies and moved troopsSource: Jay Feyerabend, master's thesis (opens in a new tab), James Madison University (2021)

Bookmarks: Massachusetts.

Known issues

No known issues.

Inquiry

Compelling question

Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

Pick the questions that suit your class. Each one lists the MapMaker tools it uses, linked to how-to videos.

  1. Where did the war begin?

    Open the Massachusetts bookmark and click the Lexington and Concord diamond, then Boston. Note the dates, and the winner from the symbol color and legend. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?

    Zoom out to see all 21 battles, from Quebec to South Carolina, and sort them into two lists by year. Which colonies saw fighting each year, and what changed?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  3. Why New York?

    Turn on Key Port Cities (it sits inside the Revolutionary War Battlefields group) and zoom to New York City. Compare its harbor and rivers with Boston's. What could a navy do from New York?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. How did 1776 end?

    Zoom in near New York City until the numbered turning points show, and follow circles 4 and 5. Find Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton, and note who won each. Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton.

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a route drawn with Sketch, or bookmarks saved for a short talk.

Tools: Sketch, how-to video: Sketch on a Map (opens in a new tab) · Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

Open the map in MapMaker: 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Before you start

British soldiers marched out of Boston to seize weapons that colonists had stored at Concord. The fighting that followed started the American Revolution. For the next two years, the British army and navy and the new Continental Army, led by George Washington, fought over the colonies' cities, rivers and harbors.

Reading the map

Diamonds mark battles: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory. Each diamond is placed at the battle's usual location, but the fighting covered a wider area: gray shaded areas show the battlefield, and areas with diagonal stripes show the core, where the fighting was heaviest. Zoom in to see white numbered circles: five turning points, numbered in the order they happened.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Where did the war begin? Open the Massachusetts bookmark. Click the diamond at Lexington and Concord. When was it fought? Use the legend to find out who won. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord: miles
  2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776? Zoom out until you can see every diamond, from Quebec to South Carolina. Click each one and write its name under the year it was fought. Which colonies had battles in 1775? Which in 1776? What changed?
  3. Why New York? In Map layers, turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (it's inside Revolutionary War Battlefields). Zoom in on New York City. Compare its harbor and rivers with Boston's. What could a navy do from New York?
  4. How did 1776 end? Zoom in on New York City until the numbered circles appear, then follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton. Who won each? Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton: miles

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two places on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about 1775–1776 that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Before class

No preparation beyond checking the map opens on student devices. Students don't need accounts to explore it; saving their own copy needs a sign-in.

Answer notes

1. Where did the war begin?

Lexington and Concord, April 19, 1775, an American victory. The siege of Boston ran from April 19, 1775, to March 17, 1776. Boston to Concord is about 16 miles (26 km) in a straight line, so expect answers of 15–17 miles.

2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?

YearAmerican victoriesBritish victories
1775 (8 battles)American victories: Lexington and Concord, Boston (siege) and Gloucester (Massachusetts); Fort Ticonderoga and Crown Point (New York); Great Bridge (Virginia)British victories: Bunker Hill (Massachusetts); Quebec (Quebec)
1776 (13 battles)American victories: Moores Creek Bridge (North Carolina); Sullivan's Island and Breach Inlet (South Carolina); Gwynn's Island (Virginia); Trenton (New Jersey)British victories: Brooklyn, Valcour Island, Pell's Point, White Plains, Fort Washington (New York); Fort Lee, Mount Holly (New Jersey); Newport (Rhode Island)

Fighting began around Boston, then spread along the coast. From August 1776 most battles were in New York and New Jersey.

3. Why New York?

The American Battlefield Trust says the city's "central position in the American Colonies and its port made it vital to commerce and a key strategic location", and that British warships could "dominate the river waterways that cut through New York City." The British left Boston in March 1776 and won at Brooklyn on August 27. (Battle of Brooklyn, American Battlefield Trust (opens in a new tab))

4. How did 1776 end?

Fort Washington (November 16) and Fort Lee (November 20) were British victories; Trenton (December 26) was an American victory. New York City to Trenton is about 52 miles (84 km) in a straight line.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The early war was fought in Massachusetts.” By the end of 1776 the map shows battles in seven colonies and in Quebec.
  • “The winner is the side that lost fewer soldiers.” Bunker Hill is shown as a British victory, yet its pop-up says the British had twice as many casualties as the Patriots.
  • “The Americans lost every battle in 1776.” The map shows American wins in the South that year, such as Moores Creek Bridge and Sullivan's Island, as well as Trenton.

Key words

  • siege
  • militia
  • Continental Army
  • Loyalist
  • harbor
  • campaign
  • retreat

Standards

CodeStandard
TX 8.4(C)Standard: Explain the issues surrounding important events of the American Revolution, including declaring independence; fighting the battles of Lexington and Concord, Saratoga, and Yorktown; enduring the winter at Valley Forge; and signing the Treaty of Paris of 1783
TX 8.10(A)Standard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
TX 8.10(C)Standard: Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
FL SS.8.A.3.6Standard: Examine the causes, course, and consequences of the American Revolution
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Standard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Standard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past

About this map

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Trails WestWhat it shows: Seven trails west: Oregon, California, Mormon Pioneer, Old Spanish, Santa Fe, Butterfield Overland and Pony Express, each in its own color in the legend. Each pop-up gives the trail's name and a short history with dates.Source: National Geographic Education, from National Park Service trail information
Transcontinental Railroads completed by 1911 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Five transcontinental lines named in the legend: Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Union Pacific, Central Pacific and Southern Pacific.   • Open 2026-10-12 Trails West pop-up (Oregon): Gives the years 1840 to 1860, then says many travelers were "fleeing the American Civil War (1861-1865)", which began after that period.

Inquiry

Compelling question

How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

Pick the questions that suit your class. Each one lists the MapMaker tools it uses, linked to how-to videos.

  1. Where did the trails begin?

    Click three trails and note where each started and ended. Most began in Missouri: why there?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. How far, and how many?

    Open the Oregon Trail pop-up for its length and how many people used it. Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the trail's length.

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  3. Whose land?

    Turn on Indigenous Territories and zoom in until the nations' names appear, then follow one trail. Was the West empty land when the trails were built?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  4. From trails to rails

    Turn on the Railroads group. Which trail does the first transcontinental line follow most closely? Click a thin gray railroad line to see when it was in operation (the transcontinental lines have no pop-up).

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

Open the map in MapMaker: Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Before you start

In the 1800s, hundreds of thousands of people from the eastern United States went west in wagons, looking for farmland, gold or a place to practice their religion freely. A journey along one of the trails could take months. Later in the century, railroads were built across the West.

Reading the map

Each trail is a dotted line in its own color; the legend names them. Railroads and Indigenous Territories are off when the map opens: turn them on in Map layers. Thick colored lines are the transcontinental railroads, and thin gray lines are other railroads. Each Indigenous nation's territory is shaded in its own color, and its name appears when you zoom in. The territories are approximate and aren't listed in the legend.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Where did the trails begin? Click three of the dotted trail lines. Where did each one start and end? In which state do most of the trails start?
  2. How far, and how many? Click the Oregon Trail (find its color in the legend). How long was it, and how many people traveled it? Why is the trail longer than a straight line? Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon: miles
  3. Whose land? In Map layers, turn on Indigenous Territories. Zoom in until the nations' names appear, then follow one trail. Was the land the trail crossed empty? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?
  4. From trails to rails In Map layers, turn on Railroads. Which trails does the Union Pacific and Central Pacific line follow most closely? Click a thin gray railroad line: when was it in operation?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about the journey west that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Before class

The Railroads and Indigenous Territories layers are off when the map opens; students turn them on in the layer list. The map has no bookmarks, so students zoom and pan to find places.

Answer notes

1. Where did the trails begin?

TrailFromTo
OregonFrom: Independence, MissouriTo: Willamette River valley, near Portland, Oregon
CaliforniaFrom: Independence, Missouri, and Omaha, NebraskaTo: Northern California
Mormon PioneerFrom: Near Omaha, NebraskaTo: Salt Lake City, Utah
Santa FeFrom: MissouriTo: Santa Fe, New Mexico
Pony ExpressFrom: St. Joseph, MissouriTo: Sacramento, California
Butterfield OverlandFrom: St. Louis, Missouri, and Memphis, Tennessee, via Fort Smith, ArkansasTo: San Francisco, California
Old SpanishFrom: Abiquiú, New MexicoTo: Los Angeles, California

Most start in Missouri, at the western edge of the settled states and on the Missouri River, where travelers could buy supplies before setting out.

2. How far, and how many?

The pop-up gives about 2,000 miles (3,219 km) and 300,000 to 400,000 people between 1840 and 1860. The straight line is about 1,500 miles (2,420 km). The trail is longer because it followed rivers for water and grass, and crossed the Rocky Mountains through passes.

3. Whose land?

No. The layer shows Indigenous nations' territories across all the land the trails crossed. The map's description notes that Manifest Destiny overlooked the Indigenous and Hispanic people already living in the West, and that trails and railways crossing Native lands led to conflict and great loss of land.

4. From trails to rails

It runs close to the California and Mormon Pioneer trails across Nebraska, Wyoming, Utah and Nevada. The first transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869, the year the California Trail pop-up says that trail's use ended. The Pony Express pop-up says it stopped in October 1861, when a transcontinental telegraph line was completed.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The West was empty before settlers arrived.” The Indigenous Territories layer shows nations' lands across the whole region the trails crossed.
  • “Everyone went west on the Oregon Trail.” The map shows seven trails, to Oregon, California, Utah, New Mexico and Southern California.
  • “The Pony Express lasted for decades.” Its pop-up says it ran for 18 months, from April 1860 to October 1861.

Key words

  • Manifest Destiny
  • emigrant
  • trail
  • transcontinental railroad
  • telegraph
  • Indigenous nation

Standards

TX 8.6(B)Standard: Explain the political, economic, and social roots of Manifest Destiny
TX 8.6(C)Standard: Analyze the relationship between the concept of Manifest Destiny and the westward growth of the nation
TX 8.11(A)Standard: Analyze how physical characteristics of the environment influenced population distribution, settlement patterns, and economic activities in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
FL SS.8.A.4.1Standard: Examine the causes, course, and consequences of United States westward expansion and its growing diplomatic assertiveness
C3 D2.Geo.7.6-8Standard: Explain how changes in transportation and communication technology influence the spatial connections among human settlements and affect the diffusion of ideas and cultural practices
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Standard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past

About this map

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
US States and Territories 1850What it shows: States and territories in four legend groups: free states, free by compromise, slave states, and slave by compromise. By 1850, the Northern states had ended slavery or passed laws to end it, but in the South slavery was legal and growing. More than 3 million people were enslaved in the United States. Each time a new state joined the Union, Congress argued over whether slavery would be allowed there.

States and territories are shaded brown if they were free and green if they allowed slavery; the paler shades mean free, or slave, because of a compromise.   3. The internal slave trade Follow the solid black lines of the Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade. Which states do the routes connect? The lines have no arrows, so use what you have learned: in which direction were enslaved people forced to move?

Answer notes

1. Free states and slave states

16 free states (including Iowa and California) and 15 slave states (Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky and Missouri). The map also draws West Virginia separately; count it as part of Virginia. In the East the line runs along the southern border of Pennsylvania (the Mason–Dixon line) and then the Ohio River.

2. The Missouri Compromise

Missouri. It was admitted as a slave state in 1820 even though most of it lies north of 36°30′ North; Maine was admitted as a free state at the same time to keep the Senate balanced (from the layer's notes).

3. The internal slave trade

The routes run from the older slave states of the Upper South, such as Virginia, Maryland and Kentucky, south and west to the Deep South, such as Mississippi, Louisiana and Alabama. North across Ohio, Indiana and Illinois to Lake Erie and the Detroit River, at places such as Cleveland, Ashtabula, Toledo and Detroit, and on to Canada (Chatham and Toronto in Ontario, Montreal in Quebec). Before you start

In November 1860, Abraham Lincoln was elected president. He opposed the spread of slavery into the western territories, and Southern slave states began to leave the Union to form the Confederate States of America. In April 1861, Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter, a Union fort in South Carolina, and the Civil War began.

Reading the map

States are shaded by side in 1863: shades of blue for the Union and shades of brown for the Confederacy; the legend explains each shade. A white dashed line marks the boundary between the two sides. Thin dark gray lines are railroads built by 1863. Diamonds mark battles: blue for a Union victory, brown for a Confederate victory, white if neither side won. Bigger diamonds mean more soldiers were killed, wounded, captured or missing. Tan shaded areas show the land each battlefield covered, and areas with diagonal stripes show where the fighting was heaviest.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. A nation divided Use the legend. Which states left the Union before the attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861? Which left after? Which slave states stayed in the Union?
  2. The border states Zoom to Washington, D.C. Which two states border it? What would have happened to the capital if Maryland had left the Union?
  3. Railroads, North and South Compare the railroads (thin dark gray lines) north and south of the white dashed boundary between the Union and the Confederacy. Which side had more? Why would railroads matter in a war?
  4. Where were the battles? Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania. Click the tan shaded areas of two battlefields to read their names. Where were most battles fought? Name a battle fought in a Union state.

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about the Civil War that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Answer notes

1. A nation divided

GroupStates on the map

West Virginia split from Virginia and joined the Union as a state in June 1863, which is why it appears on this 1863 map.

2. The border states

Maryland and Virginia. Virginia joined the Confederacy, so if Maryland had seceded, the Union capital would have been surrounded by Confederate states.

3. Railroads, North and South

The North had a much denser railroad network, so it could move soldiers, food and weapons faster and farther. The map shows lines, not mileage; for figures, use the 1860 census.

4. Where were the battles?

Most battlefields on the map are in the Confederate states, above all Virginia. Antietam (Maryland, 1862) and Gettysburg (Pennsylvania, 1863) were fought in Union states.

  • “All slave states joined the Confederacy.” The legend shows five slave states that stayed in the Union: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri and West Virginia.

Before you start

In 1862, Union forces captured New Orleans and Memphis, two cities on the Mississippi River. Between the two, the Confederates still held part of the river, including the city of Vicksburg, Mississippi. In spring 1863, Union General Ulysses S. Grant set out to capture it.

Reading the map

The yellow pin is Vicksburg. Dark pins mark places on Grant's route, each with its name. Railroads are thin dark lines with short cross marks, like a track; they appear when you zoom in, and they include lines built after the war. Civil War Battlefields is off when the map opens: turn it on in Map layers. Its diamonds mark battles: blue for a Union victory, gray for a Confederate victory, yellow if neither side won.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Why Vicksburg? Open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Vicksburg is the yellow pin on the Mississippi River. Zoom in until the railroads appear: where does the railroad from Vicksburg lead? Why would both sides want the city?
  2. Grant's route Find the dark pins for Milliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards. Which side of the river is each on? Why did Grant march south before crossing the river? Measure the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend: miles
  3. The battles of May 1863 In Map layers, turn on Civil War Battlefields. Click the diamonds between Bruinsburg and Vicksburg and list the battles in order by date.
  4. Splitting the Confederacy Zoom out to see the whole Mississippi River. Vicksburg surrendered on July 4, 1863. Which Confederate states were cut off west of the river?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two places on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Answer notes

1. Why Vicksburg?

Vicksburg stands on high bluffs over a bend in the Mississippi, so its guns controlled traffic on the river. A railroad ran east to Jackson, linking the river to the rest of the Confederacy. Whoever held Vicksburg controlled the river between the Confederacy's eastern and western states.

2. Grant's route

Milliken's Bend, New Carthage and Hard Times are on the Louisiana (west) side; Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards are in Mississippi. Vicksburg's guns and the swamps north of the city made a direct attack too hard, so Grant marched south down the Louisiana side and crossed the river at Bruinsburg on April 30, 1863, then turned northeast. Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend is about 33 miles (53 km) in a straight line.

BattleDates

RaymondDates: May 12, 1863

Champion HillDates: May 16, 1863

Grand Gulf (April 29, 1863) was the Union navy's failed attack just before the crossing at Bruinsburg.

Texas, Arkansas and most of Louisiana. After Port Hudson, Louisiana, surrendered on July 9, 1863, the Union controlled the whole river.

  • “Grant attacked Vicksburg straight across the river.” The key places show he marched south on the Louisiana side and crossed at Bruinsburg, well south of the city.

  • “Gettysburg was the only turning point of July 1863.” Vicksburg surrendered on July 4, 1863, the day after Gettysburg ended, and gave the Union the Mississippi.

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did the Constitution balance large and small states, and how close did it come to being rejected?

Open the map in MapMaker: We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791

Before you start

In 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia and wrote the Constitution. Large and small states disagreed about how many votes each should have in Congress. The Constitution would take effect only when nine states had ratified it, each at a special convention.

Reading the map

The map has no place names: click a pie or a state to see its name. Pies on the states show the people in 1790: blue for free, orange-red for enslaved, and bigger pies for more people. Three layers are off when the map opens. In House seats in 1793, darker blue means more seats. In Ratifying the Constitution, each pie sits where a state's convention met: blue for votes to ratify, orange-red for votes against, and labels give the order each state ratified. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Who lived where in 1790? Open The states in 1790 bookmark and click the pies. Which state had the most people? In which states were more than a quarter of the people enslaved?
  2. Seats in Congress In Map layers, turn on House seats in 1793. Which state had the most seats in the House of Representatives, and which the fewest? How many senators did every state have?
  3. The three-fifths clause Under the three-fifths clause, three of every five enslaved people were counted when House seats were shared out. Click Virginia and South Carolina: how many seats would each have had if enslaved people had been counted in full, or not at all? Which states gained seats by counting people who could not vote? Virginia: seats with the three-fifths clause; if enslaved people were not counted.
  4. How close was ratification? Turn off Population in 1790 and House seats in 1793, and turn on Ratifying the Constitution. Click the pies to find the three closest votes. Why does North Carolina have two pies?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

Teacher notes

Before class

House seats in 1793, House seats today and Ratifying the Constitution are off when the map opens. The basemap has no place names, so students click a pie or a state to see its name. The population pies and the ratification pies overlap, so question 4 asks students to turn the population layer off.

Answer notes

1. Who lived where in 1790?

StatePeopleEnslavedShare enslaved
South CarolinaPeople: 249,073Enslaved: 107,094Share enslaved: 43.0%
VirginiaPeople: 747,610Enslaved: 292,627Share enslaved: 39.1%
GeorgiaPeople: 82,548Enslaved: 29,264Share enslaved: 35.5%
MarylandPeople: 319,728Enslaved: 103,036Share enslaved: 32.2%
North CarolinaPeople: 393,751Enslaved: 100,572Share enslaved: 25.5%

Virginia had the most people, 747,610 (Kentucky was counted separately). Massachusetts, which then included Maine, was next with 475,327.

2. Seats in Congress

Virginia had the most, 19 of the 105 seats; Delaware had the fewest, 1. Every state had 2 senators. This was the Great Compromise: seats in the House by population, which suited the large states, and an equal Senate, which protected the small ones. House seats were one for every 33,000 people counted.

3. The three-fifths clause

StateSeats (three-fifths)If counted in fullIf not counted
VirginiaSeats (three-fifths): 19If counted in full: 22If not counted: 13
North CarolinaSeats (three-fifths): 10If counted in full: 11If not counted: 8
MarylandSeats (three-fifths): 8If counted in full: 9If not counted: 6
South CarolinaSeats (three-fifths): 6If counted in full: 7If not counted: 4
New YorkSeats (three-fifths): 10If counted in full: 10If not counted: 9
GeorgiaSeats (three-fifths): 2If counted in full: 2If not counted: 1
KentuckySeats (three-fifths): 2If counted in full: 2If not counted: 1

Counting three-fifths of enslaved people gave these states 15 more seats than not counting them, at the same ratio of one seat per 33,000 people: 105 seats in all instead of 90. Virginia alone gained 6. Enslaved people were counted, but they could not vote.

4. How close was ratification?

StateVoteDateOrder
Rhode IslandVote: 34–32Date: May 29, 1790Order: 13th
New YorkVote: 30–27Date: July 26, 1788Order: 11th
MassachusettsVote: 187–168Date: February 6, 1788Order: 6th
VirginiaVote: 89–79Date: June 25, 1788Order: 10th
New HampshireVote: 57–47Date: June 21, 1788Order: 9th

By share of the vote the closest were Rhode Island, New York and Massachusetts; by number of votes, Rhode Island (2), New York (3), then Virginia and New Hampshire (10 each). New Hampshire was the ninth state, enough to put the Constitution into effect. North Carolina's first convention, at Hillsborough, voted 184–84 on 1 August 1788 neither to ratify nor to reject the Constitution until amendments were considered; a second, at Fayetteville, ratified in November 1789, after Congress had proposed the Bill of Rights. The map's 1788 pie shows this as 83 for and 184 against: see Known issues.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The three-fifths clause gave enslaved people a share of representation.” It gave slaveholding states more seats, not enslaved people a voice: they could not vote. Virginia's pop-up shows 19 seats under the clause, against 13 if enslaved people had not been counted.
  • “Every state ratified the Constitution easily.” Rhode Island ratified by 34 to 32 and New York by 30 to 27, and North Carolina's first convention refused to ratify.
  • “Large states had more senators.” Every state had two senators; only House seats followed population.

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: Where in our community do people use their rights and carry out their responsibilities?

Open the map in MapMaker: Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live

Before you start

In 1791, ten amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, were added to the Constitution. They protect rights such as freedom of speech, religion and the press, the right to gather peacefully, and the right to a fair trial. Citizens also have responsibilities to their community and their country.

Reading the map

Blue lines are the boundaries of congressional districts for the 119th Congress (2025–2027); click inside one to see who represents it. National Register of Historic Places is off when the map opens: turn it on in Map layers and zoom in to see its diamonds, colored by type of place. Put your pins on public places, not homes.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Who represents us? Zoom to your community. The blue lines are the boundaries of congressional districts. Click inside your district: who represents it in the House of Representatives, and which party do they belong to? How many districts does your state have?
  2. Rights in public places Zoom in near your school. Sketch a pin on four public places, such as a courthouse, a polling place, city hall, a library, a newspaper office or a place of worship. Label each pin with a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there. Choose public places, not homes.
  3. Responsibilities Add a pin for each place where people carry out a responsibility as citizens, such as voting, serving on a jury or paying taxes. Which of these responsibilities are required by law, and which are voluntary?
  4. History where we live In Map layers, turn on National Register of Historic Places. Zoom in until the diamonds appear, and click two near your school. Is either a public building, such as a courthouse, post office, school or library? Which right or responsibility does it connect with?

Your answer: Use your map to answer the big question. Choose the three places that best show rights and responsibilities in your community, and explain your choices.

Looking back

What did the map show you about your own community that you hadn't noticed before?

Teacher notes

Before class

Students need to find your community on the map; the Topographic basemap has place names. Without a sign-in, sketches aren't saved, so students can download an image or export a PDF to keep the work. Pins on public places keep students' addresses private. The midterm elections are on 3 November 2026, and the map's description lists the states that have new district lines for them.

Answer notes

1. Who represents us?

It depends on where you are. The pop-up names the representative and party for the 119th Congress (2025–2027); a seat that has changed hands since the layer was updated may differ. A state's number of districts equals its House seats after the 2020 census, for example California 52, Texas 38 and Florida 28; six states have one. The map's description lists the states with new district lines for the elections on 3 November 2026.

2. Rights in public places

PlaceRightAmendment
Newspaper officeRight: Freedom of the pressAmendment: First
Place of worshipRight: Free exercise of religionAmendment: First
City hall or a public squareRight: Peaceable assembly and petitioning the governmentAmendment: First
LibraryRight: Freedom of speech and of the press: reading and sharing ideasAmendment: First
CourthouseRight: Due process; a speedy, public trial by jury, with a lawyerAmendment: Fifth, Sixth and Seventh

A polling place connects with voting, which later amendments protect (the 15th, 19th and 26th) rather than the Bill of Rights.

3. Responsibilities

Required by law: obeying laws, paying taxes, serving on a jury when called and, for most men aged 18 through 25, being registered with the Selective Service System. Voluntary: voting, staying informed, volunteering and taking part in community meetings. Voting is a right and a responsibility, but no federal law requires it.

4. History where we live

It depends on where you are. Courthouses connect with jury service and the right to a fair trial; post offices and newspaper buildings with sharing news and ideas; schools and libraries with staying informed. If nothing is listed nearby, zoom out to the nearest town.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The Bill of Rights lists all of a citizen's rights.” The Ninth Amendment says other rights are kept by the people, and later amendments added rights, such as the voting rights in the 15th, 19th and 26th.
  • “Voting is required by law.” No federal law requires it. Serving on a jury when called and paying taxes are required.
  • “Everyone in a state votes for the same representative.” Each district elects its own representative; senators are chosen by the whole state.

Big question: How did the first political parties divide the country?

Open the map in MapMaker: Presidential Elections, 1796 and 1800

Before you start

George Washington belonged to no party, and in 1796, as he prepared to leave office, he warned Americans against parties. By then two had formed: the Federalists, led by John Adams and Alexander Hamilton, and the Democratic-Republicans, led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. Each elector cast two votes for president, and the runner-up became vice president.

Reading the map

The map has no place names: click a pie to see the state's name. Each pie shows how a state's electors voted: orange for John Adams (Federalist) and blue for Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican). Bigger pies mean more electors. Each elector cast two votes; the pop-up lists the other candidates. Election of 1800 is off when the map opens. Pink squares mark two Supreme Court cases. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia, and territories aren't shown.

Questions

  1. The election of 1796 Open The sixteen states bookmark and click the pies for 1796. Which part of the country mostly voted for Adams, and which for Jefferson? Which states split their votes?
  2. The election of 1800 In Map layers, turn off Election of 1796 and turn on Election of 1800. Which large state changed from Adams to Jefferson? Which states split their votes this time?
  3. A tie In 1800 each elector still cast two votes. Click Virginia and New York. Who received the same number of votes as Jefferson? Why did the House of Representatives have to choose the president? Jefferson: votes. Aaron Burr: votes.
  4. The Supreme Court Click the two pink squares: Marbury v. Madison (1803) and McCulloch v. Maryland (1819). For each, write the question the Court answered and why the ruling matters.

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about the first political parties that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Teacher notes

Before class

Election of 1800 is off when the map opens; with both elections on, the pies overlap. The basemap has no place names, so students click a pie to see the state. The pies show only Adams's and Jefferson's votes; the pop-ups list the other candidates (in 1796 the minor ones are grouped as others, as in the National Archives table).

Answer notes

1. The election of 1796

Adams won every elector's vote in New England, New York, New Jersey and Delaware. Jefferson won the South and the West: Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Kentucky and Tennessee, and most of Pennsylvania. Maryland (Adams 7, Jefferson 4), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 14, Adams 1), Virginia (Jefferson 20, Adams 1) and North Carolina (Jefferson 11, Adams 1) split. Adams won with 71 votes to Jefferson's 68, so Jefferson, the runner-up, became vice president.

2. The election of 1800

New York's 12 electors voted for Adams in 1796 and for Jefferson in 1800. Without that change Adams would have had 77 votes to Jefferson's 61; instead Jefferson had 73 and Adams 65. In 1800 Maryland split 5–5, and Pennsylvania (Jefferson 8, Adams 7) and North Carolina (Jefferson 8, Adams 4) split.

3. A tie

Aaron Burr, Jefferson's own running mate. Each elector voted for both, so Jefferson and Burr tied with 73 votes each, and the tie sent the election to the House of Representatives, which chose Jefferson on 17 February 1801. The 12th Amendment (1804) then gave electors separate votes for president and vice president.

4. The Supreme Court

CaseQuestionWhy it matters
Marbury v. Madison (1803)Question: Could the Supreme Court order Secretary of State James Madison to deliver William Marbury's commission?Why it matters: Judicial review: courts can decide whether laws and actions follow the Constitution ("A Law repugnant to the Constitution is void").
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)Question: Could Congress charter a national bank, and could a state tax it?Why it matters: Congress may use appropriate means to carry out its powers, and federal law overrides state law, so Maryland's tax was void.

Marbury grew out of the change of party in 1801: Marbury was one of John Adams's last-minute appointments, and Jefferson's administration did not deliver his commission.

Common misunderstandings

  • “Voters chose the president directly.” Electors did, and states chose their electors in different ways. In 1796 and 1800 each elector cast two votes.
  • “Adams and Jefferson ran together.” They were rivals from different parties: in 1796 Jefferson, the runner-up, became Adams's vice president.
  • “The 1800 tie was between Jefferson and Adams.” It was between Jefferson and his own running mate, Aaron Burr, with 73 votes each.

Open the map in MapMaker: The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

Before you start

In 1803 the United States bought France's claim to a huge area west of the Mississippi River. President Thomas Jefferson sent the Corps of Discovery, led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, to explore it and look for a water route to the Pacific Ocean. The expedition set out in 1803 and returned in 1806.

Reading the map

The map has no place names: click an area or a line to see its name. Green is the land Britain gave up to the United States in 1783; yellow is the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. Edges of the purchase settled later have other colors or stripes. A line follows the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail, and small symbols mark the Corps' approximate campsites. United States Watersheds and Biomes are off when the map opens and show today's landscape.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. A bigger country Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark. Compare the yellow Louisiana Purchase with the green land of the United States in 1783. About how much bigger did the country become? Click the Louisiana Purchase: how much land was it, and what did it cost? Size: about million acres. Price: $ million.
  2. Why New Orleans? In Map layers, turn on United States Watersheds. Click inside the large brown outlines along the Ohio and Missouri rivers. Which river regions are they? Their rivers flow into the Mississippi and past New Orleans to the Gulf of Mexico. Why did control of New Orleans matter to American farmers?
  3. Up the Missouri Open the Up the Missouri bookmark and follow the trail up the Missouri River. Turn off United States Watersheds, turn on Biomes, and click along the route. Which biome covers the Great Plains? Why do you think the Corps traveled along rivers?
  4. Across the Rockies Open the Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark. Where does the trail leave the Louisiana Purchase? Was the Pacific coast part of it? Measure the straight-line distance from the trail's eastern end, at Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to the Pacific coast. Straight-line distance: miles. The trail itself is about 4,900 miles long.

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers. Remember that the people already living on this land aren't on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about the Louisiana Purchase that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer and bookmark names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Before class

Watersheds and Biomes are off when the map opens. The basemap has no place names, so students may need help finding Pittsburgh and New Orleans. The trail and campsite layers come from the National Park Service, and the questions don't depend on their pop-ups. The map has no layer of the Native nations the Corps met: the National Park Service says there were more than 50, and the final answer should recognize them.

Answer notes

1. A bigger country

About 530 million acres for $15 million (from the pop-up), roughly doubling the size of the United States. Some edges were settled later: the strip given to Britain in 1818 (striped), and the parts that came with Texas in 1845 and the Mexican Cession in 1848.

2. Why New Orleans?

The Ohio, Upper Mississippi and Missouri river regions all drain into the Mississippi. Farmers in Kentucky, Tennessee and Ohio shipped their crops downriver, so whoever held New Orleans could close their route to market. In 1802 Spanish officials there stopped Americans storing goods in the port, and Jefferson tried to buy New Orleans before France offered all of Louisiana.

3. Up the Missouri

Temperate grasslands, savannas and shrublands cover the Great Plains along the Missouri. The Corps traveled upriver by boat: the rivers gave a route, water and food, and the campsites line the riverbanks.

4. Across the Rockies

The trail leaves the purchase in the Rocky Mountains, at the Continental Divide; the Pacific Northwest was not part of the purchase. The straight-line distance is about 2,200 miles (expect 2,100–2,300), less than half the trail's 4,900 miles, because the Corps followed winding rivers and mountain passes. The National Park Service says the expedition met more than 50 Tribal Nations along the way.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The United States bought the land from the people who lived there.” It bought France's claim. Native nations lived on and governed much of the land, which the United States later took through treaties and force.
  • “Lewis and Clark explored only the Louisiana Purchase.” West of the Rocky Mountains the trail leaves the purchase: the Pacific Northwest was not part of it.
  • “The Louisiana Purchase was the state of Louisiana.” It stretched from the Gulf of Mexico to British North America, covering all or part of 15 of today's states.

New Orleans was fought on January 8, 1815, two weeks after the Treaty of Ghent was signed; news of the peace hadn't yet crossed the Atlantic. Horseshoe Bend was fought against the Red Stick Creeks, not the British, though the layer calls the other side British.

3. Florida and a new border

Spain ceded East and West Florida (the United States already held much of West Florida), and the United States took on $5 million of Americans' claims against Spain instead of paying a price. The border ran up the Sabine River, north to the Red River, west along the Red to 100° W, north to the Arkansas River, up the Arkansas to its source, north to 42° N, and west along 42° N to the Pacific. The treaty was ratified in 1821.

4. New nations and the Monroe Doctrine

Before December 2, 1823 the United States had recognized Colombia, Mexico, Buenos Ayres and Chile. Monroe warned European powers not to set up new colonies in the Americas or interfere with the newly independent nations, and said the United States would stay out of Europe's wars. Haiti, independent since 1804, was not recognized until 1862.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The United States won the War of 1812 and gained land.” The Treaty of Ghent returned the borders to where they were before the war, and the map shows American and British victories on every front.
  • “The Battle of New Orleans won the war.” It was fought on January 8, 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent was signed on December 24, 1814.
  • “Every battle was against British soldiers.” The battles in Alabama were part of the Creek War, fought against the Red Stick Creeks.
